answers.note: Clear process with a good coverage table and action list, but the national curriculum reference is a loose paraphrase of topic areas (including some KS2 content) rather than the actual statements.
Thorough and practical: atomic NC statement codes, an I/D/A/R term-by-term grid with example rows, explicit ordering and progression checks, and prioritised actions with owners and dates.

Excellent end-to-end method with coded NC strands, depth codes, a worked RAG grid, team moderation of tags and a phased action plan, marred only by a small slip implying KS3 computing is optional in Year 9.
Well-timed agenda that sums to 45 minutes, turns each concern into a testable question, includes an error-hunt demo, a six-step checking protocol and a logged two-week trial with a set review.

Concise, correctly timed plan with hands-on practice on teachers' own worksheets, but the error check is only 'solve every question' and it never explicitly separates teacher planning use from student use of AI.

Strongest facilitation: clarifies what 'lazy' means, gives sceptics checking roles, runs an error hunt, provides a six-step checking routine, model prompt, commitment card and a dated review with a stop option, all within 45 minutes.
Clear, concise and practical on data protection, accuracy and allowed uses, but says nothing about being transparent with students or parents.
Very comprehensive on GDPR, accuracy, bias, JCQ rules and transparency, but at ten sections it reads as a full policy rather than guidance staff can quickly follow.
Covers every point in a staff-friendly format, with a four-question check before feedback reaches students, explicit transparency, a pilot and a ready-to-use handbook paragraph.
